newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Rescuers hold hands with Australia slide survivor.
newsitem.headline: Rescuers hold hands with Australia slide survivor.

text.p: Rescuers on Saturday reached a man who survived more than two days entombed between huge concrete slabs in the rubble of two Australian ski lodges smashed by a landslide.
"All reports are that he is in great spirits," ambulance spokesman Dane Goodwin told reporters.
"He has been able to move his arms around so we believe it's like a mini-tomb in there," he said.
But rescuers said it could take hours before the man, unofficially identified as ski instructor Stuart Diver, was pulled from the mass of metal, concrete and mud.
"One of the rescuers managed to put his clenched fist through a small cavity which is 10 cm (four inches) in diameter and has been able to hold hands with the victim," a policewoman told Reuters.
She said rescuers were pumping warm air into the cavity and had managed to feed the survivor warm fluid, a balanced solution of electrolytes and nutrients.
"They managed to pass a small torch (flashlight) through to the man and it has enabled him to describe his present situation to the rescue team," she said.
The landslide buried 20 people near midnight on Wednesday at Thredbo, 400 km (250 miles) south of Sydney.

Three deaths have been confirmed but only one body has been recovered. The trapped man, whose wife is one of those believed buried in the rubble, is sandwiched between concrete slabs, three on top and one below.
Police said he was suffering from lacerations and hypothermia, but gave no more details.
"We will not know (more) until we open up the hole more and get paramedics in there," Goodwin said.
Rescuers said they were still about two metres (six feet) from the man.
Fire brigade spokesman Ian Krimmer said rescuers were still digging through soil, rock, concrete and bricks in order to free the man and the rescue operation may take up to two hours.
"It is still an inch by inch process," Krimmer said.
Krimmer said rescuers believed the area where the man was found may be a bedroom, as mattresses and blankets had been recovered, suggesting others may still be found.
"We are in an area now where there is a chance of other survivors," Krimmer said. "So from time to time you are seeing equipment being shut down, so we can utilise our seismic listening devices."
Rescuers had all but given up hope of finding a survivor from the twisted wreckage of the Carinya and Bimbadeen lodges and the fear of more landslides frequently suspended the rescue operation.
Police on Friday had virtually ruled out the chance of finding a survivor, saying the likelihood was "infinitesimally small."
But just after dawn on Saturday rescuers heard muffled sounds and detected muscle movement under a concrete slab. "A miracle has occurred...," police superintendent Charlie Sanderson told reporters.
Frantic rescuers dug by hand to try to reach the trapped man. Krimmer said the man's first words to rescuers was: "I can hear you."
Rescuers trying to reach the man had to frequently stop operations due to the possibility of more landslides and slippages caused by movement of material.
"If what we do under there for example forces the slab to drop our efforts will be vain," Sanderson said.
